questions.solution: Correct Option D - AV node with slow and fast pathway: This patient most likely suffers from paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT) , most commonly caused by atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT). AVNRT is a tachyarrhythmia caused by a dysfunctional AV node with two electrical pathways, one fast with a long refractory period and one slow with a short refractory period (dual AV nodal physiology). During normal sinus rhythm, the conduction occurs via the fast pathway, and the incoming current from the slow pathway is extinguished. Typical AVNRT is triggered by an atrial premature beat (APB). An APB arrives at the AV node during the fast pathway's refractory period. The impulse is, therefore, conducted through the slow pathway, which is out of its refractory period. When the impulse reaches the distal junction of the two pathways, the fast pathway has recovered its excitability, and the impulse can travel retrograde. The impulse reaches the atria, leading to an almost simultaneous depolarization of the atria and ventricles. The current reenters the slow pathway. A reentry circuit is created with anterograde conduction across the slow-conducting pathway and retrograde conduction in the fast pathway resulting in sustained tachycardia. Alternative electrical conduction pathways (one fast and one slow) in the atrioventricular node (AV node) are the underlying cause of AVNRT. The presence of an extra, fast accessory pathway occasionally leads to a non-extinguishable circulating electrical impulse (reentrant circuit) within the AV node that activates the atria and ventricles simultaneously and at a rapid rate. This produces episodic symptoms of palpitations, dyspnea, chest pain, dizziness and syncope. Incorrect Options: Option A - Macroreentrant rhythm in the right atrium through the cavotricuspid isthmus: This statement is incorrect, as one of the underlying atrial flutter mechanisms is a macroreentrant rhythm in the right atrium. While atrial flutter can cause symptoms of cardiac arrhythmias, such as palpitations or syncope, it is usually asymptomatic. It is distinguished on the ECG by the sawtooth appearance of P waves ("flutter waves"). Option B - Preexcitation of the ventricles: This statement is incorrect as the underlying mechanism of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome is the preexcitation of the ventricles via a congenital accessory conduction pathway between the atria and ventricles (WPW). Although WPW can cause PSVT, the ECG would show a shortened PR interval and a delta wave in the QRS complex. WPW is also a less common cause of PSVT than AVNRT. Option C - Fibrosis of the sinoatrial node and surrounding myocardium: This statement is incorrect, as the underlying mechanism of sick sinus syndrome is fibrosis of the sinoatrial node and surrounding myocardium (SSS). While dizziness and syncope are symptoms of SSS, they are usually caused by sinus node dysfunction, which causes persistent sinus bradycardia (rather than supraventricular tachycardia ) and is more common in elderly patients. It is characterized by a prolonged QT interval on the electrocardiogram (ECG), representing the time it takes for the heart to depolarise and repolarize during a single heartbeat. LQTS is caused by gene mutations that encode ion channels or their regulatory proteins responsible for maintaining a normal cardiac rhythm. These mutations alter the flow of ions across the cell membrane, leading to a delay in the repolarisation of the ventricles and an increased risk of ventricular arrhythmias. There are several types of LQTS, each with a distinct genetic mutation and clinical presentation. The most common type, LQTS1, is caused by a KCNQ1 gene mutation and is associated with an increased risk of sudden cardiac death during physical activity or emotional stress. LQTS2 is caused by a mutation in the KCNH2 gene and is associated with an increased risk of cardiac events during sleep or rest. LQTS3 is caused by a mutation in the SCN5A gene and is associated with a high risk of arrhythmias during exercise or bradycardia. The diagnosis of LQTS is based on a combination of clinical criteria, family history, and genetic testing. Treatment typically involves lifestyle modifications, such as avoiding triggers that can prolong the QT interval, and medication, such as beta-blockers or sodium channel blockers, which can reduce the risk of arrhythmias. In some cases, implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) may be necessary to prevent sudden cardiac death. He has chronic atrial fibrillation treated with a drug that prolongs the QT interval. During cardiac stress testing, an ECG shows progressive shortening of the QT interval as the heart rate increases. Which of the following drugs is this patient most likely taking?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Dofetilide: This patient is most likely taking dofetilide. Dofetilide is a class III antiarrhythmic used to maintain normal sinus rhythm in patients with chronic atrial fibrillation. Class III antiarrhythmics inhibit potassium channels responsible for repolarizing the cardiac membrane . Delayed repolarization prolongs the duration of the cardiac action potential and the effective refractory period, which results in QT interval prolongation on ECG. All class III antiarrhythmics, except amiodarone, exhibit reverse use-dependence, as seen during this patient's cardiac stress testing. Accordingly, these drugs have decreased antiarrhythmic effects at faster heart rates and are associated with developing torsades de pointes at slower heart rates. Incorrect Options: Option A - Diltiazem: This statement is incorrect as diltiazem is a class IV antiarrhythmic used for rate control in patients with atrial fibrillation. Class IV antiarrhythmic drugs inhibit slow calcium channels mediating cardiac pacemaker depolarization. This inhibition decreases the ability of cardiac pacemaker cells to reach the threshold potential and decreases conduction velocity. As a result, the duration of the effective refractory period increases, which results in PR interval prolongation on ECG. Class IV antiarrhythmics do not affect the QT interval. Option B - Lidocaine: This statement is incorrect as lidocaine is a class IB antiarrhythmic used to treat ventricular arrhythmias; it is not used to treat atrial fibrillation. Class IB antiarrhythmics block sodium channels in cardiac myocytes and reduce the duration of the action potential. They do not affect the QT interval. Moreover, while class IB antiarrhythmics exhibit use dependence in very rare cases, they do not exhibit reverse use dependence. Option C - Flecainide: This statement is incorrect as flecainide is a class IC antiarrhythmic used to convert atrial fibrillation to sinus rhythm. Class IC antiarrhythmics block sodium channels in cardiac myocytes and prolong the effective refractory period in the atrioventricular node . Although this class of antiarrhythmics has little effect on ventricular repolarization, the QT interval is minimally prolonged due to the increase in the QRS duration. @Neet_pg_bot

Adenosine causes a transient atrioventricular (AV) block by increasing potassium efflux from cells, which causes hyperpolarization, decreased calcium influx, and decreased levels of intracellular cAMP. The brief AV block (usually < 15 secs) can cause chest pain and a feeling of impending doom. Other side effects of adenosine include hypotension, flushing, bronchospasm, bradycardia, and nausea. Prolonged asystole is rare but also a potential complication. Theophylline and caffeine are adenosine receptor antagonists that can inhibit the effect of adenosine. Incorrect Options: Option A - Severe headache: This statement is incorrect as severe headache is a common side effect of nitrates (e.g., nitroglycerin, isosorbide dinitrate), which release nitric oxide in smooth muscle cells, resulting in vasodilation and increased intracranial pressure. Other side effects of nitrates include hypotension, reflex tachycardia, and syncope. Severe headaches are not a common side effect of adenosine, which this patient received. Option B - Sedation: This statement is incorrect as sedation is a known side effect of beta-blockers (e.g., metoprolol, labetalol) and class IB antiarrhythmics (e.g., lidocaine, mexiletine). questions.solution: Correct Option C - Heart Block: Sinus bradycardia, 2 nd and 3 rd degree heart blocks, heart failure, cardiogenic shock, high grade peripheral arterial disease, as well as metabolic acidosis and tumor pheochromocytoma are the contraindications of the beta blocker, atenolol. It should not be administered to patients who have histories of asthmatic disease, bronchospasms, or other obstructive airway disorder . It might be administered in those with no other option usually combined with a bronchodilator. When giving to patients suffering from diabetes or thyroid pathologies, great care is required because the drug's effects might hide the symptoms of hypoglycemia and thyrotoxicosis; also, suddenly stopping atenolol might cause a thyroid storm . Atenolol can also pass the barrier of placenta and is linked to intrauterine growth restriction, thus physicians should be extremely careful regarding their use during pregnancy . Newborns can get hypoglycemia and bradycardia , hence it is against advice using this drug during the nursing period . Beta-blockers have been linked to anaphylactic cases . Hence those who have a history of hypersensitivity to atenolol or other agents should not use atenolol . Incorrect Options: Option A - Tachycardia: This is usually not a contraindication to the use of atenolol. Kidney disease: A lower than usual blood supply to the organ might be caused by a kidney injury or by arteries that are too narrow. Renin production may be elevated as a result of this problem . Renin then goes and stimulates the body to produce chemicals that can impact blood pressure, such as angiotensin II. Adrenal glands can malfunction, leading to an imbalance of adrenal hormones that can lead to a number of pathologies or diseases. These ailments may consist of: Pheochromocytoma Primary aldosteronism or Conn's syndrome Cushing's disease. Hyperparathyroidism and Thyroid issues can also be the reason behind secondary hypertension. Aortic coarctation : This condition causes the aorta to tighten . Normal blood flow is impeded due to this coarctation. Obstructive sleep apnea is also a known cause of secondary hypertension. Secondary hypertension can also be caused by drug side effects, such as: hormonal birth control, anabolic steroids, drugs that are non-steroidal anti-inflammatory (NSAIDs), weight reduction pills, stimulants, antidepressants, immunosuppressive drugs and decongestants . Depending on the illness or disease that is functioning in conjunction with high blood pressure, the symptoms of secondary hypertension can be variable . The need for a secondary hypertension screening will depend on a number of factors . These elements consist of: Individuals under 30 years old who present with high blood pressure or hypertension who have no family history or other high blood pressure risk factors. Individuals with resistant hypertension experience persistently high blood pressure although they are receiving the recommended dosages of at least three antihypertensive medications. Obesity: Over time, persons with high blood pressure who are overweight do not respond to medication Symptoms or signs that are pointing to a possible underlying problem such as adrenal or thyroid malfunction . Anomalies in the lab, like excessive calcium or low potassium. This buildup can lead to partial or complete blockage of the arteries, resulting in reduced blood flow to the heart and other vital organs. questions.solution: Correct Option A - Hypomagnesaemia: Electrolyte abnormalities, including hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, and hypokalemia, are involved in causing torsades de pointes. Magnesium deficiency causes membrane instability. Magnesium deficiency can cause QT interval lengthening due to Na+-K+ pump inhibition and a change in membrane potential, which puts a person at risk for life-threatening polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or Torsades de pointes. Intravenous magnesium is given to all patients with torsades de pointes, irrespective of the magnesium levels. 8 mmol of magnesium is given over 15 mins, followed by 72 mmol of magnesium in 24 hours should be given. If the patient does not respond to magnesium, then atrial pacing is done which suppresses the arrhythmia through rate-dependent shortening of the QT interval. Incorrect Options: Option B - Hypercalcemia: Hypercalcemia is not associated with torsades de pointes. Hypercalcemia causes a shortening of the QT interval . Torsades de pointes occur in conditions that result in prolongation of the QT interval. The plateau phase of the ventricular action potential is prolonged due to hypocalcemia. Due to the prolonged time that calcium ion channels are kept open, late calcium influx and early after-depolarisations can occur, which result in QT prolongation . Option C - Hyperkalemia: Hyperkalemia is not associated with torsades de pointes. Hypokalemia is associated with torsades de pointes. The extended ventricular repolarization, delayed conduction, and aberrant pacemaker activity caused by hypokalemia can result in arrhythmogenicity . A pathogenic element in developing torsade de pointes is prolonged cardiac repolarization, reflected by a prolonged QT interval. Hypokalemia causes QT prolongation. Option D - Hyponatremia: Hyponatremia is not associated with torsades de pointes. Patients with hyponatremia present with nausea, stupor, malaise, seizures, and coma. @Neet_pg_bot
